references_named: Augusto de Campos / Noigandres group / Brazilian concrete poetry (1950s)
rationale: The mechanism is genuinely web-native and only-the-web: CSS hyphens:auto forces the layout engine's dictionary to insert render-only break-hyphens that exist nowhere in the DOM, and the readback panel proves it by counting zero hyphens in textContent while the screen shows them. Concept and execution collapse cleanly (P1): the word that says it cannot be broken is broken, live, by the engine. The lang switch and resize re-break the same words differently, staging the chance/order axis (P5) and giving the work a double reading (P7) — surface gag plus a concrete-poetry argument about authorship surrendered to the typesetter. Restraint is exemplary (P3): one CSS property, three words, a readback. Tone is dry and intelligent, not edgy. G6 holds: the catalogue has no prior work that interrogates browser hyphenation as material; closest neighbours (Modernipsum, Silencio, Un Coup de Dés) operate on different mechanisms.
reservations: Narrative placement is decent but not pinpointed to a specific prior y-a-v-a work it answers — the concrete-poetry lineage is invoked rather than a catalogue entry. The novelty is real but the underlying CSS behaviour is well-known to web practitioners, so the 'aha' lands more on the art-historical argument than on a new web mechanism per se.
revision_suggestion: Consider naming a specific prior y-a-v-a work this answers (e.g., Modernipsum as the language-toy precedent, or Silencio as the source-vs-render precedent) to tighten the twenty-year-argument placement.
